title: Tail-focused loadbench protocol and clock synchronization playbook
content:
Purpose and scope
This document prescribes a lightweight, repeatable loadbench protocol with an explicit focus on tail-latency behavior while preserving throughput fidelity. It complements our steady-state throughput playbooks by prescribing: (1) machine-level preconditions (thermals, power, clocks), (2) precise clock synchronization across load generators and targets, (3) a staged warmup that surfaces tail sensitivity, and (4) artifact capture for reproducible postmortems.

Why tail-focused?
Most throughput runs report p50/p95 but miss microburst-induced p99+ regressions that affect production SLAs. This protocol attempts to: 1) make tail events deterministic enough to reproduce, 2) isolate causes (batching, KV cache coldness, kernel jitter, thermal throttling), and 3) produce small, analyzable artifacts for regression triage.

High-level recipe (summary)
- Prepare and document the environment (driver, CUDA, image sha, BIOS, power profile).
- Ensure sub-ms clock alignment across all load generators and hosts (PTP preferred).
- Run a 3-stage warmup: kernel-warm -> KV/prefix cache prime -> steady plus calibrated microbursts.
- Keep RNG seeds, workload trace, and client pacing config in run metadata.
- Capture telemetry at 1s or sub-second granularity: request-level latency, batching stats, GPU metrics (NVML), OS metrics, perf counters.
- Run at least 5 independent repetitions using different seeds, then report bootstrap CI on p99 and throughput.

1) Environment preconditions
- OS and driver: document kernel version, NVIDIA driver version, and CUDA toolkit. Use identical images (image sha).
- Power management: disable automated power cycling/fan control changes during runs. If using power caps, explicitly set and document NVML power-limit.
- GPU clocks: pin stable GPU clock profile when possible (nvidia-smi -ac) and record. Thermal headroom: allow 20 minutes of idle time after any maintenance that could leave fans/temps out of band.
- Background processes: stop cron jobs, monitoring agents that may induce jitter. If unavoidable, capture their activity in the telemetry.

2) Clock synchronization (critical for cross-host tail analysis)
- Use PTP (ptp4l + phc2sys) for hosts in the same rack/segment; fall back to NTP only if PTP is unavailable, but annotate runs clearly.
- Validate sync: run a quick one-minute timestamp exchange test between load generators and target and ensure max skew < 200 microseconds. Save the skew log.
- Rationale: without tight clocks you cannot align microburst injection times and trace-level latencies across hosts.

3) Load generator setup and RNG hygiene
- Use deterministic RNG seeds for payload selection and inter-arrival jitter; store seed in metadata.
- Client pacing options: Poisson arrival (exponential inter-arrival) for naturalistic traffic; deterministic uniform spacing for reproducible peak throughput comparisons.
- For tail-focused runs, employ a hybrid: baseline Poisson at target throughput plus scheduled deterministic microbursts (see warmup section).

4) Warmup protocol (3 stages)
- Stage A: Kernel + runtime warm (5–10 minutes). Run a small set (10–50) of representative requests with target sequence lengths to warm dynamic libraries, JIT caches, and CUDA kernels. Goal: get runtime into steady instruction paths.
- Stage B: Model/KV prefix cache prime (10–20 minutes depending on dataset). Re-play a short trace at 0.2x target throughput but with full diversity of prompt prefixes to populate KV/prefix caches and tokenization caches.
- Stage C: Tail probe warmup (5–10 minutes): ramp to target throughput and inject calibrated microbursts (short high-intensity windows described below) to reveal initial tail sensitivity.
- After warmup, allow 60–120s stabilization before capturing final steady-state runs.

5) Microburst design (how to exercise tail)
- Microburst shape: short window (200–800ms) with 3–5x target request rate; follow with 2–5s baseline recovery.
- Schedule: insert microbursts at deterministic offsets (e.g., 30s, 90s, 150s) so runs are directly comparable.
- Vary burst intensity and duration across repeats to probe different bottlenecks (e.g., small spikes exercise scheduling; longer spikes exercise memory pressure/eviction).

6) Metrics and observability capture
- Request-level: request_id, start_ts, end_ts, payload_size, token_count, model_version, batch_size, batching_delay_ms, queue_time_ms.
- Aggregates: throughput (reqs/s and tokens/s), p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latencies with sliding-window series, average batch occupancy, dropped/failed requests.
- System telemetry: nvml GPU util, mem used, power draw, GPU clocks, temperature; CPU steal time, loadavg, network tx/rx; kernel trace events for context switches.
- Perf counters (optional): kernel/memory stalls, L2 cache metrics when investigating model-specific stalls.
- Sampling frequency: for tail analysis we prefer 200–1000ms granularity for system telemetry and per-request logs at the request granularity.

7) Artifact capture and run metadata (minimum reproducibility set)
- loadgen command line and version (git sha), seed, and config file.
- model artifact id and quantization flags, runtime binary sha, Docker image sha.
- host list and roles (loadgen vs target), PTP/NTP logs, skew test output.
- nvml logs and a VM-level top/ps snapshot before/after run.
- a single-json summary that includes key run scalars and links to raw logs.

8) Repetition and statistical reporting
- For any regime we recommend at least 5 independent runs with varied RNG seeds and microburst phase offsets.
- Use bootstrap to compute 95% CI for p99 and throughput. Report both per-run time-series and aggregate CI.
- Flag runs where environmental skew (clock, power) exceeded thresholds and exclude or annotate them.

9) Quick triage checklist when you see an elevated tail
- Are GPU temps climbing and clocks stepping down? Check NVML timelines.
- Is batch occupancy spiking? Look at batching_delay and batch_size histograms.
- Did the microburst align with garbage-collection or other host-level jobs? Correlate p99 spikes with process activity.
- Is the p99 correlated with token length distribution change? Compare token_count histograms pre/post spike.

10) Run naming and storage conventions
- name: bench-YYYYMMDD-<model>-<target-rps>-burstprofile-<seed>-<runid>
- store: s3://redwood-bench/artifacts/<name>/ with subfolders: nvml/, perf/, loadgen/, summary.json

11) Example commands (illustrative)
- loadgen: ./bench-client --config conf/baseline.json --seed 12345 --burst-schedule conf/bursts.json --target-rps 800 --output ./out/name
- clock test: ./clock-sync-check --targets hosts.txt --duration 60 --max-skew-us 200 --out sync-log.json

12) Notes and caveats
- This protocol accepts longer setup time in exchange for reproducible tail signal. For quick eyeballing, shorter warmups can be used but you should mark the run as exploratory.
- Microbursts intentionally stress scheduling paths; they are not a substitute for realistic user traffic traces. Use both trace-driven replay and microburst probing for full coverage.

Appendix: minimal run checklist (copyable)
- [ ] Document image sha, driver, CUDA, model sha
- [ ] Confirm PTP skew <200us and attach sync log
- [ ] Set and record NVML power caps and GPU clock profile
- [ ] Run stage A,B,C warmups and timestamp completion
- [ ] Save loadgen config and RNG seed
- [ ] Start telemetry collectors (nvml, perf, sysstat) at 1s granularity
- [ ] Run N=5 repetitions; collect summaries and bootstrap CI

Questions and open items
- Investigate automating microburst calibration: a small feedback loop to tune burst intensity so p95 increases by ~10–20% (search space: burst size, duration).
- Evaluate if sub-ms clock sync across cloud instances can be standardized in images.

If you run this protocol or make changes, add a short experiment note to the run folder describing any deviation from the checklist.
